founded.what: The year Joseph Krug founded the house at Reims, after learning Champagne at the house of Jacquesson.

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, as the library teaches: Krug owns two walled vineyards and more, yet buys grapes from a wide network of growers and makes the wine itself at Reims.

story: Joseph Krug (1800 to 1866), born in Mainz, learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own at Reims in 1843. In 1848, as the house tells it, he began a notebook setting down his creed: to make the fullest expression of Champagne every year, whatever the weather, by blending the wines of many plots and many years. His son took over at his death in 1866, the year the house moved to the Rue Coquebert. The blend was sold as Private Cuvée until 1978, when the house renamed it Grande Cuvée. Beside it Krug made vintage wines; at the 1976 harvest, by its own account, it decided to make a rosé, first presented in 1983; and from the walled Clos du Mesnil, bought in 1971, a Chardonnay of one vineyard first made from the 1979 vintage. Clos d'Ambonnay, of Pinot Noir, followed with the 1995 vintage. In January 1999 the Rémy Cointreau group, which had held a large share of the house for years, sold it to LVMH. Krug kept fermenting in small old oak casks while most houses turned to steel, and it built a library of reserve wines for its cellar master to draw on. In the 2010s it began to print an Édition number on the front label, from the 163ème.

style.line: Weight, nuttiness and length rather than lightness: every base wine ferments in small old oak casks, each plot apart, and a large library of reserve wines is blended back.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, all three in Grande Cuvée, from plots across the villages of Champagne, each kept apart as its own wine; the house also owns the walled Clos du Mesnil and Clos d'Ambonnay.
style.reserve: A library of reserve wines from many years: 42 per cent of the 172ème Édition, from ten other years, and 31 per cent of the 173ème, by the house.
style.vessels: Small, old oak casks for the fermentation of every base wine, each plot on its own, by the house.
style.lees: About seven years in the Reims cellars for Grande Cuvée, by the house's Édition notes.

nv.name: Krug Grande Cuvée
nv.note: Krug makes no other non vintage white: the prestige cuvée is itself the wine guests know, a multi vintage blend rebuilt each year as a numbered Édition.

cuvee.name: Krug Grande Cuvée

first.what: The year the house's multi vintage blend, sold until then as Private Cuvée, was renamed Grande Cuvée.

cuvee.rhythm: Made anew every year as an Édition, each built around one harvest: the 172ème around 2016 and the 173ème around 2017, by the house. The Édition number has been printed on the front label since the 163ème.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, in shares that change with each Édition; Pinot Noir led the 172ème, then Chardonnay, then Meunier, by the house.
cuvee.sites: Plots across the villages of Champagne, each kept apart as its own wine, and a library of reserve wines from many years: 146 wines from 11 years, the oldest of 1998, for the 172ème Édition by the house.
cuvee.making: Each plot ferments on its own in small, old oak casks rather than steel, so that every wine can be judged apart before blending. More than a hundred and twenty wines from more than ten years are blended, reserve wines making about a third to over two fifths of the whole: 42 per cent for the 172ème and 31 for the 173ème, by the house. The bottles then rest about seven years on their lees in the Reims cellars.
cuvee.lees: About seven years in the Reims cellars, by the house's Édition notes.
cuvee.young: Toasted brioche, roasted hazelnut and candied lemon peel over ripe pear, with marzipan, gingerbread and honey in the house's own notes, and a broad, almost vinous weight.
cuvee.aged: Drinks well on release and keeps developing for a decade or two after it, gaining toffee, coffee and dried fig.
cuvee.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold, within the 9 to 12 the house gives; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

table.house45: Krug was founded at Reims in 1843 by Joseph Krug, a German from Mainz who had learned his trade at Jacquesson. His idea was to make the fullest Champagne every year, whatever the weather, by blending many plots and many years. Every base wine ferments in small old oak casks, and the house keeps a deep library of reserve wines. That is why Krug tastes broad and nutty, with brioche and hazelnut. Guests meet the house through Krug Grande Cuvée, rebuilt each year as a numbered Édition. Beside it stand Krug Vintage and two walled vineyards, Clos du Mesnil and Clos d'Ambonnay.
table.house10: Krug is the Reims house of 1843 that ferments every wine in small old oak casks and blends many years into Grande Cuvée.
table.cuvee45: Krug Grande Cuvée is the house's whole idea in one bottle. It blends more than a hundred and twenty wines from over ten years and from plots across Champagne. All three grapes are in it: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier. Each plot ferments apart in small old oak casks, and reserve wines make up about a third or more of the blend. It rests about seven years in the Reims cellars. It tastes of toasted brioche, roasted hazelnut and candied lemon peel. The Édition number on the label tells you which year's blend you hold. Pour it at nine to eleven degrees in a wine glass, never a narrow flute.
table.sale: Krug Grande Cuvée drinks like a mature white Burgundy with bubbles, a blend of more than a hundred wines from over ten years. Shall I open a bottle and pour it in wine glasses?
table.cuvee10: Krug Grande Cuvée is a multi vintage blend of more than a hundred and twenty wines, fermented in small old oak casks.
table.cuvee20: Krug Grande Cuvée is a multi vintage Champagne, rebuilt each year as a numbered Édition from more than a hundred and twenty wines of over ten years. Each plot ferments in small old oak casks and the blend rests about seven years, for brioche, hazelnut and candied lemon peel.

guests.q: Is Grande Cuvée a vintage Champagne?
guests.a: No. It carries no vintage on purpose: each Édition is built around one harvest and blended with reserve wines from many other years, then aged about seven years.

guests.q: What does the Édition number mean?
guests.a: It counts the yearly creations of the blend, not a year: the 172ème Édition is built around the 2016 harvest and the 173ème around 2017.

guests.q: Does Krug make anything above Grande Cuvée?
guests.a: Beside it stand Krug Vintage and two single walled vineyards, Clos du Mesnil of Chardonnay and Clos d'Ambonnay of Pinot Noir. Grande Cuvée is the cuvée the class sheet names, and the house's own idea.

traps: The class sheet prints Grand Cuvée; the label reads Krug Grande Cuvée, with an e, because cuvée is a feminine word.
Grande Cuvée alone means Krug to most guests and examiners; the class sheet also prints Grand Cuvée for Ayala, whose prestige cuvée is Perle d'Ayala.
Grande Cuvée carries no vintage, yet it spends longer in the cellar than many vintage Champagnes.
Clos du Mesnil is Chardonnay from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger; Clos d'Ambonnay is Pinot Noir from Ambonnay. Neither is a form of Grande Cuvée.

sheet.note: The sheet drops the e of Grande; cuvée is feminine, so the label reads Grande Cuvée. The label adds the Édition, the blend's place in the yearly line, such as 172ème Édition.

questions.q: A guest asks for the multi vintage prestige cuvée of the Reims house Joseph Krug founded in 1843. Which wine is it?
questions.exp: Grande Cuvée is Krug's multi vintage blend. La Grande Année is Bollinger's vintage wine, Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's blend of three vintages and La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's.

questions.q: In what does Krug ferment every base wine, as the house describes it?
questions.exp: Krug ferments each plot apart in small, old oak casks, so every wine can be judged before blending. It kept to casks while most houses turned to stainless steel tanks.

questions.q: Around which harvest is Krug Grande Cuvée 172ème Édition built?
questions.exp: The 172ème is built around 2016, with 146 wines from 11 years, the oldest of 1998. The 173ème is built around the 2017 harvest.

report: Built on the published flagships record (codex58, key krug, refuted on 12 November 2026) and the library's p-krug: no fact of either is contradicted, and the story, the glass, the ageing and the traps keep the published wording where they overlap.

Added from the house's own Édition pages: the 172ème built around 2016 from 146 wines of 11 years back to 1998, with 42 per cent reserve wines and Pinot Noir leading; the 173ème around 2017, 150 wines of 13 years, 31 per cent reserve; the 165ème's serving range of 9 to 12 degrees Celsius, which the record reports beside the published 9 to 11 it keeps.

The rosé: the published record says the house added a rosé in the 1970s, 1976 by its own account; the house's rosé page dates the decision to the 1976 harvest and the first showing to 1983, which this record states, a refinement and not a contradiction.

The sale to LVMH in January 1999 is in Wikipedia and Wine Spectator; when the Rémy Cointreau group first took its share differs (1969 by one Decanter interview, the early 1970s by another account), so it is not dated.
Clos d'Ambonnay's first vintage of 1995 is the library's and the published record's; it was not searched again.
The name change of 1978 is the published record's; one merchant gives 1979, which the record does not follow. A narrower bottle neck from 1978 is in one account and is left out.

style.dosage is empty: the house's pages read give no figure for Grande Cuvée (one merchant's 4 grams a litre for the 173ème and a data site's 9 grams of residual sugar were not followed); style.malolactic is empty because no page read states it.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; the library's own trap says Krug is an NM house, and a refuter should read a label.

The open point of the published refuter stands and is repeated for the owner: the library's p-krug says the Édition number is on the back of the bottle, while it is printed on the front and the back carries the Krug iD.
cuvee.forms is empty: Krug Rosé, Krug Vintage and the two clos are wines of their own, not forms of Grande Cuvée, as the plan rules.

The house's own Édition notes speak of flowers and ripe, dried and citrus fruits; the record keeps only the named things, marzipan, gingerbread, hazelnut, brioche and honey, beside the published glass.

changed: story: The house dates the decision to the 1976 harvest; no source makes the rosé the wine of a Pinot Noir harvest.
